THE MAGIC BEAN CO. LIMITED
STRATEGIC REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 30 SEPTEMBER 2024
- 1 -
The directors present their strategic report for The Magic Bean Co Limited, a private company limited by shares, for the year ended 30th September 2024. During the year under review the company has continued building on the successes of the prior year, acquiring sites, and opening new stores, despite the continuing challenges posed by inflation, the cost-of-living crisis and the Gaza conflict.
Review of the business
Company revenues increased by £7.1 m to £31.7m (2023: £24.6m); EBITDA increased by £0.1m to £3.0m (2023: £2.9m). Incremental sales revenues generated proportionate increases in gross profits, which in turn were reinvested into central infrastructure including additional resource in property and operations team to accelerate new site opportunities and drive revenue and EBITDA growth across the estate. The gross profit margin improved slightly due to a slight reduction in direct supply chain costs, although the direct labour costs increased in line with national living wage inflation thereby offsetting some of the deflation seen in supply chain. The company was mindful of the cost-of-living pressures that affected its customers and was cautious implementing pricing adjustments which were necessary to mitigate some of the increased year on year costs of labour, business rates and energy contract renewals.
While the underlying business has adjusted to a ‘post-covid norm’, it remains profitable and cash generative; there was a slight downturn in sales volumes during this period which was due to a combination of customers being more cautious with their spend and some sites saw politically motivated boycotts following the Gaza conflict, which has been seen across multiple geographic markets. This resulted in the official forecast that was prepared in September 2023 being slightly downgraded mid-term during FY2024. However, the company actuals since then have met the revised forecast performance targets. We have brought forward investment in infrastructure and staff resource as we prepare the business for the next phase of growth, which we look forward to accelerating as we add more sites to our network and build relationships with key partners to make this happen.
The company started the financial year with 38 trading sites, comprising 18 Drive thru and 20 Core (Café) sites and has since made further significant capex investments on 4 new sites opened and 2 acquired sites during the year. There were 4 loss-making sites closed during the year, 2 of which related to sites with leases that expired and not renewed, with the business focussing more on higher volume drive thru sites going forward. Total Capex invested in new sites including acquisitions during the year was £3.2m, with pre-trade opex costs of £146k expensed through the profit and loss account. Additionally, the one-off closure losses on disposal on the 4 sites was £628k. However, this represents a one-off cost and ongoing there will be significant cash savings generated as these losses fall away from the bottom line and the cyclical costs of refurbishing these sites instead will be allocated to existing and pending new sites. Overall, the FY24 investment brings the total number of sites trading to 42, these being comprised of 18 Drive Thru and 24 Café’s, located across a wide territory spanning South Wales and multiple counties in the Midlands, South-West of England and North East of England.
The company is well capitalised with strong operating cashflows which are sufficient to fund organic growth and a significant £10m Revolving Credit Facility secured with HSBC, which provided additional fire power to fund acquisitions during the year.
The business has enjoyed working with HSBC UK Bank Plc this year and is grateful for the ongoing support that it has provided to the company, and it is worth noting that this facility was further increased to £15m during FY25 with an additional £2.5m option.
As with the previous year, this year has also been a productive one with a significant pipeline of new stores and opportunities secured and which we will see coming to fruition in the next financial year. The business has also been proactive by investing in resource to consolidate its property, operations, and finance teams, plus investing in the digitalisation of menu screens across its estate which will enhance the customer experience.
THE MAGIC BEAN CO. LIMITED
STRATEGIC REPORT (CONTINUED)
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 30 SEPTEMBER 2024
- 2 -
The Company continued to invest in its partners by providing ongoing training as well as focussing on their well-being and safety, enabling them to deliver the high Starbucks standard that our customers value and expect. We have continued to support generous bonus schemes for our store teams to recognise their contribution and hard work. We are pleased that a good number of our stores achieved their targets which saw several of our partners receiving bonus payments and other rewards.
We very much recognise the immense contribution our partners make to the business, working unsocial hours and in environments which are often fast paced and demanding. We would like to thank them for their hard work this year and we will continue to invest in them and create new opportunities as we grow the business.
We look forward to an even bigger FY25 and are confident the company will continue an upward trajectory of new store openings and revenue growth.
Principal risks and uncertainties
Economic Outlook
This financial year did see an easing of direct supply chain costs during the year driven partly by wider deflation in the UK economy, which saw the inflation rate drop from 4.6% at the start of the financial year (October 2023) to 1.7% at the end of the financial year (September 2024). The Bank of England also started reducing interest rates to tame inflation and ease the cost-of-living crisis, the first of the cuts saw the rate drop from 5.25% to 5% in the last two months of the financial year. The reducing interest rates will help the business reduce its variable borrowing costs on its term debt and revolving credit facility. While there has been some like for like sales decline seen in some sites, the business has increased its overall store count and therefore has still grown its revenues and remained largely profitable, when one-off store closure costs are stripped out of the profit and loss. Overall customer spending, while not quite as high as the previous year, was still strong and the businesses average transaction value increased during the year which helped partially offset some of the reduction in volume. While food and beverage spending are a necessity for people, the market remains very competitive with multiple brand offerings at different price points and some of this spending may be considered ‘discretionary’ where customers can easily switch to alternatives or change their consumption rates.
This is identified as a major risk where customers can easily switch to alternatives. From time to time, it is necessary to adjust prices to address cost inflation, however we are mindful that these same inflationary pressures also affect our customers and how they may perceive the value of the brand offering and customer experience. We therefore very carefully consider our menu pricing to ensure that this fine balance is maintained. We are regularly reviewing and adjusting prices to ensure that our menus are structured to provide a ladder of different price points and we regularly compare our prices to similar competitors to ensure we are price competitive in the marketplace. We have recently undertaken a pricing review and we are monitoring sales volumes of our popular products on a like for like basis comparing to historical and seasonal equivalents to ensure that sales volumes are not being adversely affected and brand values are being maintained.
Despite a challenging start to the year overall, the business added another 4 sites (net) during the year, and these have driven revenue growth and ensured EBITDA and Cashflows remained resilient, and we believe this trend will continue into the foreseeable future.
Interest Rate Risk
In the previous year’s report, we identified risks around the volatility of the BoE rate which were realised. However, while these risks remain present, especially with some economic uncertainty caused by the impact of international tariffs, these risks appear to be easing compared with previous periods. At the start of the financial year the BoE rate was 5.25% and in August 2024 was cut to 5.0% and remained at this rate through to the financial year end. This rate appears to have passed its peak and during FY25 there have been some further cuts such that the rate at the time of writing this report stands at 4.25% with many economic forecasters projecting that rates will continue a downward trajectory to 3% over the next 12 months. While the company is well placed to meet its debt servicing costs at current rates, the gradual reductions over time will reduce its borrowing costs which is always helpful and will free up additional funds for new store investment. The company’s net debt to equity ratio, a key measure of stability and leverage, remains small and within the margins of safety and as such, the company is satisfied that debt repayments will continue to be affordable to the business.
THE MAGIC BEAN CO. LIMITED
STRATEGIC REPORT (CONTINUED)
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 30 SEPTEMBER 2024
- 3 -
Inflation Risk on Supply Chain, Supply Chain availability and Energy costs
In the previous periods we saw an increase in the costs of coffee, freight, and other business supplies because of global factors, including the post-covid ripple and the impact of the Russian invasion of Ukraine and some of these impacts have continued into this financial year with high like for like costs on some energy contracts. However, most direct supply chain costs have gradually reduced this year in line with general inflation and we have started the process of adding new stores and those with expiring energy contracts to a new supplier which offers better rates with the combined buying power of the larger franchised estate and so we expect to see some improvement on energy costs in subsequent periods. The company sources its main supplies from Starbucks UK Coffee Ltd, which itself has taken significant measures to secure the supply of products from trusted suppliers across the globe. There have also been significant increases in the costs of electricity for new energy contracts where we have opened new stores and a few existing stores where contracts on low rates have expired. On a more positive note, energy costs have also stabilised and reduced slightly compared to the highs seen last year. To this extent the company remains reasonably sheltered from the costs of energy, however it is seeking ways to reduce its future consumption to reduce costs and improve our green credentials by reviewing operations ahead of contract renewals.
Pipeline / Sector competition
The company has a pipeline of sites to ensure that there is a steady stream of new sites being developed and the company is meeting the objectives of its growth strategy. There is fierce competition for sites from rival brands and other competitors. However, the company has an experienced senior board, a growing property team and is very proactive in registering new sites and has good relationships with property partners.
Development and performance
During the year the company has closed 4 loss making sites, 2 of which were at the end of their leases and has seen the number of trading sites increase from 38 sites at the start of the year to 42 sites at the end of the financial year. The new sites comprise of 2 sites in Durham and Sunderland acquired from Starbucks UK, 4 Sainsbury’s café sites in Talbot Green, Witney, Heyford Hill and Kidlington, plus a new site in Scarborough. We look forward to seeing cost savings from the closed sites manifest in the FY25 period as well as the full year run rate contribution from the acquired and new sites opening during this period.
Future Developments
The company has a large pipeline of sites that it plans to develop and open within the next 3-4 years. Some of these sites are already exchanged or are at an advanced stage. There have also been some recent developments with EV partners and other key stakeholders, which we cannot disclose due to their strictly confidential nature. However, the company is looking forward to a bright future with many more development projects ahead.
THE MAGIC BEAN CO. LIMITED

DIRECTORS' REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 30 SEPTEMBER 2024
- 5 -
The directors present their annual report and financial statements for the year ended 30 September 2024.
Principal activities
The principal activity of the company continued to be that of a coffee shop franchise.
Results and dividends
The results for the year are set out on page 11.
Ordinary dividends were paid amounting to £300,000. The directors do not recommend payment of a final dividend.
Directors
The directors who held office during the year and up to the date of signature of the financial statements were as follows:
Mr MS Reed
Mr L R Esfahani
Financial instruments
There are two significant finance facilities in existence that the company has executed with it’s bankers HSBC UK Bank Plc ;
Term Loan
During November 2019 the company refinanced its term loan and asset finance facilities with HSBC UK Bank Plc into a new term loan of £4.856m, with a 7-year amortisation profile, the facility being renewed after 5 years.
The interest rate is HSBC Variable + BoE.
Facility Agreement
During May 2022, the company entered into a £10m Revolving Credit Facility Agreement with HSBC UK Bank Plc, which subject to pre-drawdown conditions and ongoing covenant performance criteria being met, enables the company to utilise up to £10m in additional facilities to fund the opening of new stores.
The facility is reviewed on an annual basis, and also requires the company to make quarterly compliance declarations to the bank on a rolling-12 month basis, coupled with 12 month look-forward cashflow statements.
The maximum term of the facility is 4 years with all borrowings in the facility being repayable to the bank on or before the 4th anniversary of the date of the Agreement.
The interest rate on amounts borrowed is HSBC Variable + BoE.
The facility charges the company a Non-Utilisation Fee which is determined as a fixed percentage (the HSBC ‘Margin’) applied the amount of the facility that remains undrawn.
Disabled persons
Applications for employment by disabled persons are always fully considered, bearing in mind the aptitudes of the applicant concerned. In the event of members of staff becoming disabled, every effort is made to ensure that their employment within the company continues and that the appropriate training is arranged. It is the policy of the company that the training, career development and promotion of disabled persons should, as far as possible, be identical to that of other employees.
THE MAGIC BEAN CO. LIMITED
DIRECTORS' REPORT (CONTINUED)
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 30 SEPTEMBER 2024
- 6 -
Employee involvement
The company's policy is to consult and discuss with employees, through unions, staff councils and at meetings, matters likely to affect employees' interests.
Information about matters of concern to employees is given through information bulletins and reports which seek to achieve a common awareness on the part of all employees of the financial and economic factors affecting the company's performance.
There is no employee share scheme at present, but the directors are considering the introduction of such a scheme as a means of further encouraging the involvement of employees in the company's performance.
Future developments
The company has a large pipeline of sites that it plans to develop and open within the next 4-5 years. Some of these sites are already exchanged or are at an advanced stage. There have also been some very recent developments with EV partners and other key stakeholders, which we cannot disclose due to their strictly confidential nature. However, the company is looking forward to a bright future with many more development projects ahead.
Corporate governance
WBV Limited were appointed as auditor to the company and in accordance with section 485 of the Companies Act 2006, a resolution proposing that they be re-appointed will be put at a General Meeting.
Energy and carbon report
As the company has not consumed more than 40,000 kWh of energy in this reporting period, it qualifies as a low energy user under these regulations and is not required to report on its emissions, energy consumption or energy efficiency activities.
Statement of disclosure to auditor
So far as each person who was a director at the date of approving this report is aware, there is no relevant audit information of which the company’s auditor is unaware. Additionally, the directors individually have taken all the necessary steps that they ought to have taken as directors in order to make themselves aware of all relevant audit information and to establish that the company’s auditor is aware of that information.
On behalf of the board
Mr L R Esfahani
Director
30 June 2025

Accounting policies
Company information
The Magic Bean Co. Limited is a private company limited by shares incorporated in England and Wales. The registered office is 1315 Neath Road, Hafod, Swansea, SA1 2LF.
1.1
Accounting convention
These financial statements have been prepared in accordance with FRS 102 “The Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland” (“FRS 102”) and the requirements of the Companies Act 2006.
The financial statements are prepared in sterling, which is the functional currency of the company. Monetary amounts in these financial statements are rounded to the nearest £.
The financial statements have been prepared under the historical cost convention, [modified to include the revaluation of freehold properties and to include investment properties and certain financial instruments at fair value]. The principal accounting policies adopted are set out below.
1.2
Going concern
Atruet the time of approving the financial statements, the directors have a reasonable expectation that the company has adequate resources to continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future. Thus the directors continue to adopt the going concern basis of accounting in preparing the financial statements.
The financial statements have been prepared on the basis that the company is a going concern.
The underlying business has adjusted to a ‘post-covid’ norm and during the year the Bank of England has started to reduce interest rates which will reduce borrowing costs in the company and furthermore we’ve seen a general deflation in direct supply chain costs during the current FY2025 year which in turn has improved the gross profit margin on like for like. Additionally, we are seeing energy costs reduce as we move onto new contracts with new suppliers. On the flip side, the company saw a slight downturn in sales volumes during the first few months of FY 2025 due to a combination of customers being more cautious with their spend in the cost-of-living crisis and some sites saw politically motivated boycotts following the Gaza conflict, which has also been seen across multiple geographic markets. However, since March 2025 sales volumes across most of our estate have seen a reversal of the decline and are now in like for like sales growth as compared with the similar period in 2024. In FY 2025 the business remains strong and profitable, and we expect not only to hit our financial forecasts but exceed them when we report the final position at year end. We are also developing new Starbucks Drive thru sites with three more openings planned later this summer which will further consolidate sales revenues and EBITDA profits and look forward to developing and opening multiple new Drive thru sites which are planned for FY 2026. The company is financed by a combination of the cash balances generated from trading and bank loan facilities, which were also increased recently. Therefore, the directors have a reasonable expectation, based on the company’s financial forecasts, that the company will continue to trade profitably and hence will continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future and therefore continue to adopt the going concern basis.
1.3
Turnover
Revenue is recognised to the extent that it is probable that the economic benefits will flow to the company and the revenue can be reliably measured. 1.9
Impairment of fixed assets
At each reporting period end date, the company reviews the carrying amounts of its tangible and intangible assets to determine whether there is any indication that those assets have suffered an impairment loss. If any such indication exists, the recoverable amount of the asset is estimated in order to determine the extent of the impairment loss (if any). Where it is not possible to estimate the recoverable amount of an individual asset, the company estimates the recoverable amount of the cash-generating unit to which the asset belongs.
Recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs to sell and value in use. In assessing value in use, the estimated future cash flows are discounted to their present value using a pre-tax discount rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the asset for which the estimates of future cash flows have not been adjusted.
If the recoverable amount of an asset (or cash-generating unit) is estimated to be less than its carrying amount, the carrying amount of the asset (or cash-generating unit) is reduced to its recoverable amount. An impairment loss is recognised immediately in profit or loss, unless the relevant asset is carried at a revalued amount, in which case the impairment loss is treated as a revaluation decrease.
Recognised impairment losses are reversed if, and only if, the reasons for the impairment loss have ceased to apply. Where an impairment loss subsequently reverses, the carrying amount of the asset (or cash-generating unit) is increased to the revised estimate of its recoverable amount, but so that the increased carrying amount does not exceed the carrying amount that would have been determined had no impairment loss been recognised for the asset (or cash-generating unit) in prior years. A reversal of an impairment loss is recognised immediately in profit or loss, unless the relevant asset is carried at a revalued amount, in which case the reversal of the impairment loss is treated as a revaluation increase.

Other financial assets
Other financial assets, including investments in equity instruments which are not subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures, are initially measured at fair value, which is normally the transaction price. Such assets are subsequently carried at fair value and the changes in fair value are recognised in profit or loss, except that investments in equity instruments that are not publicly traded and whose fair values cannot be measured reliably are measured at cost less impairment.
Impairment of financial assets
Financial assets, other than those held at fair value through profit and loss, are assessed for indicators of impairment at each reporting end date.
Financial assets are impaired where there is objective evidence that, as a result of one or more events that occurred after the initial recognition of the financial asset, the estimated future cash flows have been affected. If an asset is impaired, the impairment loss is the difference between the carrying amount and the present value of the estimated cash flows discounted at the asset’s original effective interest rate. The impairment loss is recognised in profit or loss.
If there is a decrease in the impairment loss arising from an event occurring after the impairment was recognised, the impairment is reversed. The reversal is such that the current carrying amount does not exceed what the carrying amount would have been, had the impairment not previously been recognised. The impairment reversal is recognised in profit or loss.
Derecognition of financial assets
Financial assets are derecognised only when the contractual rights to the cash flows from the asset expire or are settled, or when the company transfers the financial asset and substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership to another entity, or if some significant risks and rewards of ownership are retained but control of the asset has transferred to another party that is able to sell the asset in its entirety to an unrelated third party.
Other financial liabilities
Derivatives, including interest rate swaps and forward foreign exchange contracts, are not basic financial instruments. Derivatives are initially recognised at fair value on the date a derivative contract is entered into and are subsequently re-measured at their fair value. Changes in the fair value of derivatives are recognised in profit or loss in finance costs or finance income as appropriate, unless hedge accounting is applied and the hedge is a cash flow hedge.
Debt instruments that do not meet the conditions in FRS 102 paragraph 11.9 are subsequently measured at fair value through profit or loss. Debt instruments may be designated as being measured at fair value through profit or loss to eliminate or reduce an accounting mismatch or if the instruments are measured and their performance evaluated on a fair value basis in accordance with a documented risk management or investment strategy.
Derecognition of financial liabilities
Financial liabilities are derecognised when the company’s contractual obligations expire or are discharged or cancelled.

Current tax

The company’s liability for current tax is calculated using tax rates that have been enacted or substantively enacted by the reporting end date.

Deferred tax
Deferred tax liabilities are generally recognised for all timing differences and deferred tax assets are recognised to the extent that it is probable that they will be recovered against the reversal of deferred tax liabilities or other future taxable profits. Such assets and liabilities are not recognised if the timing difference arises from goodwill or from the initial recognition of other assets and liabilities in a transaction that affects neither the tax profit nor the accounting profit.
The carrying amount of deferred tax assets is reviewed at each reporting end date and reduced to the extent that it is no longer probable that sufficient taxable profits will be available to allow all or part of the asset to be recovered. Deferred tax is calculated at the tax rates that are expected to apply in the period when the liability is settled or the asset is realised. Deferred tax is charged or credited in the profit and loss account, except when it relates to items charged or credited directly to equity, in which case the deferred tax is also dealt with in equity. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset when the company has a legally enforceable right to offset current tax assets and liabilities and the deferred tax assets and liabilities relate to taxes levied by the same tax authority.

The costs of short-term employee benefits are recognised as a liability and an expense, unless those costs are required to be recognised as part of the cost of stock or fixed assets.

Termination benefits are recognised immediately as an expense when the company is demonstrably committed to terminate the employment of an employee or to provide termination benefits.

The cost and corresponding increase in equity in respect of equity-settled share-based payment transactions with employees are measured be reference to the fair value of equity instruments issued at the date of grant. Amounts are expensed on a straight line basis over the vesting period based on the estimate of shares that will eventually vest and adjusted for the effect of non market-based vesting conditions. The cost and fair value of the liability incurred in respect of cash-settled transactions is measure using an appropriate option pricing model with changes in fair value recognised in profit or loss for the period.
1.16
Leases
As lessee
Leases are classified as finance leases whenever the terms of the lease transfer substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership to the lessees. All other leases are classified as operating leases.
Assets held under finance leases are recognised as assets at the lower of the assets fair value at the date of inception and the present value of the minimum lease payments. The related liability is included in the balance sheet as a finance lease obligation. Lease payments are treated as consisting of capital and interest elements. The interest is charged to profit or loss so as to produce a constant periodic rate of interest on the remaining balance of the liability.
Rentals payable under operating leases, including any lease incentives received, are charged to profit or loss on a straight line basis over the term of the relevant lease except where another more systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern in which economic benefits from the leases asset are consumed.
